stories.headline: Rubio defends Trump's Iran war as not 'necessarily popular, but necessary'
stories.note: Rubio makes the case that Trump is putting America's security ahead of the polls on Iran.
body: Secretary of State Marco Rubio is standing behind President Trump's decision to go to war with Iran, arguing it was the only way to keep Tehran from getting a nuclear weapon.

Rubio conceded the war hasn't been popular and that it played a part in Republicans' midterm losses last week, a point Vice President JD Vance had also made. But he said Trump was responding to a very real threat, and that doing the right thing for national security isn't "necessarily popular, but necessary."

Trump has made no apologies either. Speaking to reporters Sunday, he said the war will go down in history as one of the best things his administration did, while telling "60 Minutes" he isn't looking to escalate the conflict right now.

Talks with Iran are ongoing but going nowhere fast, according to Rubio, who called Tehran's demands unrealistic and in some cases "outrageous and ridiculous." Meanwhile, Iran said it is dropping its self-imposed 2,000-kilometer limit on ballistic missile range, hours after the U.S. military launched a new task force to choke off its weapons shipments and illicit trade.
Why it matters: The administration is refusing to back down on Iran after a tough election, betting that voters will ultimately reward a president who kept a nuclear weapon out of the mullahs' hands.

stories.headline: EXCLUSIVE: Trump's FAA touts new AI-powered tool helping thousands of passengers avoid flight delays
stories.note: A concrete win for travelers that the Trump administration can point to.
body: The Trump administration's new AI-supported air traffic tool has already rerouted nearly 180 flights carrying about 24,000 passengers around congestion, trimming more than 10 minutes off flight times on average, according to Transportation Department data shared with Fox News Digital.

The FAA system, called SMART, has been running for nearly six weeks. It pulls together about 200 data streams, including weather, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing, to spot trouble before it builds and suggest better routes. DOT says it has also saved close to 80 gallons of fuel per flight on average.

In one October example, a flight with 147 passengers from Reagan National to Orlando took a route farther west that SMART recommended, cutting 11 nautical miles and six minutes. The tool doesn't fly or direct planes itself; specialists check its recommendations and local controllers decide whether to use them. It's also meant to replace the old practice of closing off big rectangles of airspace around storms.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said SMART will "slash frustrating delays, reduce stress on air traffic controllers, and lower travel prices." The rollout started in the Washington region in September, expanded to testing in Miami, Jacksonville and Atlanta in October, and the FAA aims to bring it to all 22 air traffic control centers.
Why it matters: It's a tangible, everyday win for travelers, and evidence that the administration's push to modernize air traffic control is delivering results.

stories.headline: Border Dem poised to wield ICE purse strings rejects socialist 'defund' push
stories.note: Even a key Democrat is breaking with his party's socialist wing on defunding ICE.
body: Rep. Henry Cuellar, a Texas Democrat who represents the border city of Laredo, says ICE isn't going anywhere, even as more than a dozen newly elected or reelected progressive Democrats rally around "Abolish ICE."

Cuellar is the top Democrat on the Homeland Security Appropriations Subcommittee and is in line to chair it in January, giving him real say over how ICE gets funded. He told Fox News Digital he doesn't believe in defunding ICE and thinks most Democrats don't either, though he wants more guardrails on the agency.

He also warned his party against returning to Biden-era border policy, saying Democrats can't just open the border to anyone who claims asylum, and he agreed with former Border Patrol Chief Raul Ortiz that "the Biden administration had it wrong."

Cuellar has criticized some ICE tactics and Gov. Greg Abbott's Operation Lone Star, and blamed aggressive enforcement for Democrats' gains in Texas. But he said he wants to work with President Trump and Republicans over the next two years. DHS and CBP told Fox News Digital that deportations will continue.

Why it matters: The incoming Democratic majority is already split between its socialist 'abolish ICE' wing and moderates like Cuellar, and the man who will hold ICE's purse strings is siding with enforcement.

stories.headline: Bernie Sanders warns Democrats not to spend all their time investigating Trump
stories.note: Bernie himself is warning the new Democratic majority against an investigation obsession.
body: Sen. Bernie Sanders is cautioning his fellow Democrats against spending their new majorities chasing investigations of President Trump.

On NBC's "Meet the Press," Sanders said Democrats should still pursue what he called corruption and illegal actions by the administration. But asked whether two years of probes could undercut the party's promise to lower prices, he answered, "Yes, I do." He said Democrats "cannot spend all of our time investigating Trump."

That puts him at odds with other party leaders. Incoming House Oversight leader Rep. Robert Garcia has floated investigating Trump's pardons, Elon Musk and new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has promised to bring accountability for what he calls corruption.
Sanders also called Trump erratic but admitted he is a good politician and "not stupid," saying Democrats might be able to work with him on issues like the minimum wage and health care.
Why it matters: Even Bernie sees the risk that Democrats trade their affordability pitch for an investigation spree, which is exactly the bait-and-switch Republicans plan to hammer them on.

stories.headline: Elon Musk's Austin home targeted by well-funded leftist groups aboard party buses
stories.note: Well-funded far-left groups busing protesters to a private home is a bad look for the left.
body: Three far-left nonprofits with combined 2024 revenues of about $56.1 million organized a post-election "party" outside Elon Musk's home in West Lake Hills, near Austin, on Saturday, complete with two chartered party buses, music, speeches and Cybertruck piñatas.

The organizers were VOCAL-TX, a project of New York nonprofit VOCAL-NY; the Brooklyn-based Center for Popular Democracy; and Chicago-based People's Action. About 60 people attended. Signs read "Texas is not for sale" and "Now let's tax Musk," and the mass-produced "I AM STEALING FROM YOU" Musk poster made an appearance.

A Fox News Digital investigation found these same groups helped lead last year's "Tesla Takedown" protests, which at times turned into vandalism. The Center for Popular Democracy alone reported $40.9 million in 2024 revenue, and its two co-executive directors averaged about $234,000 in total pay. The groups did not respond to requests for comment, though they have previously described their protests as organic.

The event targeted Musk's 2026 election spending, roughly $445 million to $474 million by various estimates, including about $212 million behind Ken Paxton's unsuccessful Texas Senate bid. The protesters didn't address big Democratic donors such as George Soros or Reid Hoffman.
Why it matters: It's another look at the professional, well-funded protest machine behind supposedly grassroots demonstrations, now showing up at a private citizen's home.

stories.headline: The next generation of workers is taking its talent and spending power to this Southern state
stories.note: Young workers are voting with their feet for a Southern state.
body: South Carolina drew more young adults than any other state last year, gaining a net 22,843 Gen Z residents (ages 18 to 27) through moves from other states in 2024, according to a new LendingTree analysis.

California saw the biggest net loss of Gen Z residents at 58,109, and Texas was the top landing spot for those leaving, drawing 19,287 young Californians. New Jersey and New York also posted large losses, while South Carolina, Missouri, Tennessee and Texas gained.

LendingTree analyst Matt Schulz said affordability and jobs explain much of the shift, noting South Carolina's closeness to Charlotte's growing job market. Young people, he said, want a place where they can live affordably with decent jobs and good opportunity.

The trend isn't new: IRS data cited earlier by Fox News Digital showed South Carolina added more than 59,000 residents from other states between 2022 and 2023, bringing in about $4.1 billion in income, the nation's largest per-capita gain.
Why it matters: The next generation of workers and future business owners is leaving high-cost blue states for affordable, Republican-led ones, a long-term boost for red-state economies.

stories.headline: After GOP's brutal midterms, 'Chuck Norris of Florida politics' tells party to 'get up and fight'
stories.note: A rallying cry for Republicans to regroup and fight back after the midterms.
body: Florida Lt. Gov. Jay Collins, a former Green Beret whom Gov. Ron DeSantis has dubbed the "Chuck Norris of Florida politics," has a message for Republicans after last week's midterm losses: get back up and fight.

Collins, who once operated on his own arm after it was shattered by a bullet in combat, told Fox News Digital the defeat only becomes a death blow if the party lets it. "Hard times happen. Warriors, leaders get up and fight," he said.

He pointed to Florida, which went from swing state to the largest red state on the 2028 map under DeSantis, as the blueprint. His diagnosis of the midterms is that Republicans didn't spend enough time talking to independent voters, recalling that he won his first state Senate race in Tampa by 10 points by knocking only on the doors of independents and light Democrats while being upfront about his conservative views.

Collins urged a bigger tent built on conservative values and warned the party not to "fight the last war," but to study its weaknesses and move forward with resolve. He and DeSantis are term-limited in January, and he's keeping his own next step quiet, saying only "stay tuned."
Why it matters: Florida Republicans are offering a winning playbook and a fighting spirit as the party regroups for 2028.
